name: Nicholas Mystikos
otherNames: Nicholas I of Constantinople, the first patriarch there of the name; Godfrey Henschen says he was called Nicolaus Priscus for that reason
Nicolaus Mysticus, the Latin form Angelo Mai uses
knownFor: Patriarch of Constantinople who opposed Emperor Leo VI's fourth marriage and was sent into exile for it in 907. Back in office after Leo's death, he helped govern for the boy emperor Constantine, Leo's son, and wrote the letters to Rome and to Symeon of Bulgaria that survive in Patrologia Graeca 111.
dates: Born about 852, by the patriarch lists Franz Fischer printed, which Carl de Boor reports make him 73 at his death. Made patriarch in 895 by Godfrey Henschen and Angelo Mai, or on 1 March 901 by de Boor, from the same lists and the Life of Euthymius. Exiled on 1 February 907, by de Boor; Krug and Muralt, following Symeon Magister, put it in 908, he reports. Back in office after Leo's death: in 911 by Mai, in 911 or early 912 by Henschen, in 912 by de Boor. Died 15 May, in 925 by Henschen and de Boor, in 924 by Mai
place: Constantinople, his see; Hieria, where the boat put him ashore, and Galakrenai, the Galacrenae of the Latin chronicles, which he reached on foot through deep snow; his own monastery at Galakrenai, where he was buried
role: Patriarch of Constantinople, before and after his exile; earlier the emperor's mystikos, secretary of the inner council; one of the guardians Emperor Alexander named for the boy Constantine

keyWorks.title: Letter 32, to the pope of old Rome, on the fourth marriage
keyWorks.about: his own account of the quarrel. Angelo Mai reports that Baronius took the pope for Lando and Pagi for Anastasius III; Carl de Boor says it was written in 912, after his return, to win the pope over. Mansi also prints a shorter Latin version

keyWorks.title: Twenty-six letters to Symeon, prince of the Bulgarians
keyWorks.about: written, Mai says, while Bulgarian armies stood at the walls of Constantinople. In them Nicholas pleads for peace and offers terms. Mai, citing the letters, says he at last went to Symeon himself as envoy

keyWorks.title: Homily on the capture of Thessalonica
keyWorks.about: preached in the Great Church after the city fell in 904, which Mai counts the ninth year of his patriarchate. Mai printed only a fragment, saying it holds little history

traces: The Tomus of Union was the ruling that ended the split in the church. The account Mansi prints before it says Constantine called Nicholas and all the bishops together. They granted Leo pardon after his death and banned fourth marriages from then on. Mansi prints the year 6428 from creation, that is 920; de Boor puts the agreement in 921.

Henschen's extracts from Leo the Grammarian say the whole church was brought to agreement under Romanus Lecapenus one July, with the bishops who had stood with Nicholas or with Euthymius coming back into agreement.

Angelo Mai found 163 of his letters in a Vatican manuscript, written to the emir of Crete and the caliph, Symeon of Bulgaria, popes, the emperor, princes of Armenia, Abasgia, Lombardy and Amalfi, bishops, officials and monks.
remembered: Godfrey Henschen, writing for the Bollandists, calls him a saint and finds his memory kept on 15 May in an old calendar of saints of the church of Constantinople, with other calendars giving 14 or 16 May.

Angelo Mai says his pastoral zeal, steadiness and charity seem rightly to have won him his name for holiness, and that Ephraim the chronicler called him a pious and wise monk before he was patriarch, of Italian birth and gifted for eloquence.
Carl de Boor says modern writers all built their story on his letter to Rome, and that even the other side praises him as a model shepherd who fought for his flock to the point of self-sacrifice.

uncertain: The quarrel comes from two partisan sides. His own Letter 32 was written, de Boor says, to win the pope over. The Life of Euthymius speaks for the man who replaced him. De Boor, its editor, dates it no earlier than 921, calls it a partisan work, and holds that a monk of Euthymius's Psamathia monastery wrote it within living memory. Its Greek is held only in a garbled scan, so what it says is told here as de Boor reports it.

The treason charge. The Life says a letter in Nicholas's own hand, of treasonous content, written to the rebel general Andronicus Dux, reached Leo. After that, it says, Nicholas did Leo's will and baptized the boy himself against his senior bishops. De Boor thinks the charge true, the letter real at least in sense, but grants there is no compelling proof. At one point he sets aside whether the letter was genuine or forged by Nicholas's enemies. Nicholas's own letter never mentions it. The account printed before the Tomus of Union in Mansi says Leo drove him out as a liar who had often sworn to grant the emperor's wish and as often changed his mind.

Who blessed the marriage. Nicholas writes that Leo crowned Zoe himself, as bridegroom and priest. Leo the Grammarian and Theophanes Continuatus, the chronicle that carries on from Theophanes the Confessor, name the priest Thomas, deposed for blessing them; de Boor says the Life also speaks of this priest. De Boor thinks Nicholas ran together the wedding blessing and Zoe's crowning as empress, which emperors performed themselves once the patriarch had blessed the crown.

When the legates came. Nicholas writes that the legates of Rome arrived eight or nine months after the wedding, before his arrest. In the Life, as de Boor reads it, they had not yet arrived on the day of his exile, and de Boor prefers the Life. Nicholas speaks only of Rome; Eutychius of Alexandria, the Life, and the letters of the envoy Leo Choerosphactes, as de Boor reports them, show legates of the eastern patriarchs too.

How he left office and came back. The Life and Arethas of Caesarea, as de Boor reports them, say he signed a written abdication; his own letter tells only of arrest and exile. The chronicles say Leo's brother, Emperor Alexander, recalled him; his own letters, de Boor says, say Leo did.

The dates. Henschen and Mai give 895 for his election; de Boor, 1 March 901. Henschen gives his death as 15 May 925, Mai as 924. Henschen puts Leo's death, and so the return, in 911; de Boor in 912. Leo the Grammarian gives him thirteen years in his second term, Theophanes Continuatus fourteen.

The chronicles. Leo the Grammarian and Theophanes Continuatus tell the wedding, the ban and the arrest in nearly the same words, and de Boor says the Continuator drew on one version of an older chronicle, which he calls the Logothete's, so they are not independent. Henschen calls Leo the Grammarian a contemporary eyewitness, but the manuscript's closing note, which François Combefis prints, dates his chronicle to the year 6521 from creation, that is 1013.

A far-off telling. Eutychius of Alexandria, whose Annals were written in Arabic and are held in Latin, says Nicholas told Leo that as a consecrated reader he could not take another wife, that legates of the four patriarchs with some bishops declared the marriage lawful, and that the son was born after it. He names Nicholas's successor Anthimus.
